rationale: A wins because it turns the launch into sharper accountability stories, not just product-adjacent coverage. "Your bed's health data is behind the top subscription tier" is a real consumer-affairs angle with a buyer consequence and concrete proof list; B's "Sleep trackers tell you that you snored. This bed changes its temperature while you are doing it" is useful but softer, and it leans on a trigger/response relationship the update does not fully prove. Both sets are disciplined, but A gives the founder more hard-edged paths to reporters.
gaps_in_A: "Snoring detection lands in the biohacker bed before it lands in the sleep clinic" overreaches; sleep clinics already live in snoring/oxygen territory, so the headline creates a clever contrast that may not be true.
"the sensors ship in the hardware" is stated too confidently before the proof section asks whether the sensors are physically present for non-subscribers.
The counterposition angle imports CPAP makers and home sleep-test vendors without supplied evidence; plausible beat context, but not grounded in the update.
The study angle is smart, but it probably should be marked weaker than the others until the clinic investigator is on record.
gaps_in_B: "This bed changes its temperature while you are doing it" implies real-time snoring-triggered adjustment; the update only says the bed adjusts temperature automatically.
"consumer-health or sleep-tech product reporter" is a fuzzier target than the stronger regulatory and consumer-affairs beats; that third angle risks becoming a product review.
"defensive-comment" is an odd story type for the first angle; the substance is regulatory-boundary reporting, not crisis response.
The set is cleaner than it is aggressive: it refuses the incumbent/counterposition path entirely instead of attempting a tighter, better-grounded version of it.
